title: Logical vectors
summary: Ask yes-or-no questions of every trip: compare and test membership, compare decimals safely, see what a missing value does to an answer, combine conditions, summarise TRUE and FALSE, and turn conditions into categories.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)
steps.explain: `library(tidyverse)` attaches dplyr, whose `filter()`, `mutate()` and `summarize()` this lesson feeds with logical vectors, and lubridate's `hour()`.

steps.title: Comparisons and %in%

runs.code:
trips |>
  mutate(
    rush_hour = hour(started_at) %in% c(7, 8, 16, 17, 18),
    round_trip = start_station == end_station,
    .keep = "used"
  )
alternatives: trips |> transmute(started_at, start_station, end_station, rush_hour = hour(started_at) %in% c(7, 8, 16, 17, 18), round_trip = start_station == end_station)
runs.purpose: add two yes-or-no columns: whether each trip started in a rush hour, and whether it ended where it started
runs.task: Add two columns with `mutate()`: `rush_hour`, whether `hour(started_at)` is one of 7, 8, 16, 17 or 18 (`%in%`), and `round_trip`, whether `start_station == end_station`. Keep only the columns used, with `.keep = "used"`.

steps.explain: A comparison such as `start_station == end_station` asks a question of every row at once and answers with a logical vector: `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each trip. `%in%` asks whether each value is one of a set, so `hour(started_at) %in% c(7, 8, 16, 17, 18)` marks the {n_rush} trips that started in a rush hour. `.keep = "used"` keeps only the columns the new ones were made from, so the answers are easy to check. Some `round_trip` values are `NA`; step 4 shows why.

steps.title: Decimals: near()

runs.purpose: look for trips of 2,010 metres by converting each distance to metres
runs.task: Keep the trips whose `distance_km * 1000` equals 2010, with `==`.
Do the same with `near(distance_km * 1000, 2010)` instead of `==`.

steps.explain: The first filter finds nothing, yet {n_2010} trips went 2.01 km. A computer stores most decimals, 2.01 among them, as the nearest binary fraction, so `2.01 * 1000` comes out as {stored}, not 2010, and `==` asks for an exact match. `near()` allows for that tiny difference. Use it whenever you compare numbers that came out of arithmetic.

steps.title: Missing values in comparisons

runs.purpose: count the round trips, the one-way trips and the trips whose end isn't known
keep the round trips together with the trips whose end isn't known
runs.task: Keep the trips that ended where they started, or whose `end_station` is missing (`is.na()`), joining the two conditions with `|`.

steps.explain: {n_round} trips ended where they started. For {n_unknown} the answer is `NA`: a lost bike has no end station, and a comparison with an unknown value is itself unknown. `filter()` keeps only the rows where its condition is `TRUE`, so those trips would drop out of any filter on `end_station` without a word. `is.na()` asks about missing values directly. `|` (or) is `TRUE` when either side is, so `NA | TRUE` is `TRUE`, and the filter keeps {n_either} trips.

steps.title: Combining conditions: !, & and |

runs.purpose: keep the complete trips: not lost, and with a length above zero
runs.task: Keep the trips that are not lost (missing `end_station`) or broken (`duration_min <= 0`): put `!` in front of those two conditions joined by `|`.

steps.explain: `!` turns `TRUE` into `FALSE` and back. `!(lost | broken)` keeps the trips that are neither, {n_complete} of them, the same as `!lost & !broken`: "not (A or B)" is "not A and not B". In `filter()`, a comma between conditions means `&`. Choose the form that reads most like the question you are asking.

steps.title: Logical summaries: sum(), mean(), any()

runs.code:
trips |>
  summarize(
    trips = n(),
    lost = sum(is.na(end_station)),
    share_electric = mean(bike_type == "electric"),
    any_negative = any(duration_min < 0),
    .by = member_type
  )
alternatives: trips |> group_by(member_type) |> summarize(trips = n(), lost = sum(is.na(end_station)), share_electric = mean(bike_type == 'electric'), any_negative = any(duration_min < 0))
runs.purpose: count each rider type's trips and lost bikes, find their share of e-bike trips, and check for negative lengths
runs.task: For each `member_type`, find with `summarize()`: the number of trips, `n()`; the lost bikes, `sum(is.na(end_station))`; the share on e-bikes, `mean(bike_type == "electric")`; and whether any trip has a negative length, `any(duration_min < 0)`.

steps.explain: In arithmetic, `TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0. So `sum()` of a condition counts the rows where it holds, {lost_member} lost bikes among members' trips, and `mean()` gives the share where it holds: {e_member}% of members' trips were on e-bikes, against {e_casual}% of casual riders'. `any()` asks whether at least one is `TRUE`, and `all()` whether every one is. These summaries return `NA` if a value is missing, unless you add `na.rm = TRUE`.

steps.title: Conditions into categories: case_when()

runs.code:
trips |>
  mutate(
    kind = case_when(
      is.na(end_station) ~ "lost",
      duration_min <= 0 ~ "clock error",
      start_station == end_station ~ "round trip",
      .default = "one way"
    )
  ) |>
  count(kind)
alternatives: trips |> mutate(kind = case_when(is.na(end_station) ~ 'lost', duration_min <= 0 ~ 'clock error', start_station == end_station ~ 'round trip', TRUE ~ 'one way')) |> count(kind)
runs.purpose: sort every trip into lost, clock error, round trip or one way, and count each kind
runs.task: Add a column `kind` with `case_when()`: "lost" where `end_station` is missing, else "clock error" where `duration_min <= 0`, else "round trip" where the stations match, and "one way" for the rest (`.default`). Then count the trips of each `kind`.

steps.explain: `case_when()` takes pairs of `condition ~ value` and gives each row the value of the first condition that is `TRUE`, so their order matters: a lost bike is "lost" whatever comes after, and only the trips left over reach `.default`. The {n_clock} clock errors here are trips that did reach a station. With only two outcomes, `if_else(condition, yes, no)` does the same job more briefly.
